title: Role-play lab: six client conversations
objectives: Answer six common client objections in plain words with a rupee example.
Use the module's scenario answers (Q21–Q25) as trainer-marked practice.
body_md:
In pairs. One person plays the client, the other explains — in plain words, with a rupee example.

| Client says | Explain |
| --- | --- |
| “This NFO is only ₹10, so it’s cheaper.” | NAV is the price of one unit, not a measure of value. The same percentage growth gives the same rupee result whatever the NAV level; judge a fund by its strategy, cost and fit, not by a ₹10 NAV. |
| “My SIP statement says 45% return in 3 years, so 15% a year?” | 45% is the absolute return over 3 years, not a yearly rate. For a SIP the right annualised measure is XIRR; compare it with the TRI benchmark over the same period. |
| “I want the IDCW option for monthly income.” | IDCW payouts come out of the investor’s own capital and gains, the amount and timing are not fixed, and the NAV falls by the payout. For a chosen, regular amount, compare an SWP — and refer tax questions to the client’s CA. |
| “My debt fund fell. I thought debt was safe.” | A debt fund is not an FD. Its value moves with interest rates (duration) and with borrower credit quality. Check the fund’s duration against the goal date, and promise no recovery. |
| “Why should I pay for the regular plan?” | Direct and regular plans of a scheme hold the same portfolio. The regular plan’s expense ratio includes distributor commission, which pays for guidance and service across the life of the investment. |
| “I redeemed at 2:50 pm, why did I get tomorrow’s NAV?” | For purchases, the NAV depends on when the money is received by the AMC, not when the form was submitted. The cut-off is 3 pm for most funds (1:30 pm for liquid and overnight funds); money received after it gets the next day’s NAV. |

> **Investor takeaway:** Quiz scenarios Q21–Q25 (trainer-marked): a scenario answer earns its mark if it covers at least three model points and makes no promise of returns.
example: Role-play the NFO question: ₹1,00,000 in a ₹10 NAV fund buys 10,000 units and in a ₹200 NAV fund buys 500 units; 12% growth leaves both at ₹1,12,000.
say: Say what it is in one plain sentence, give a rupee example, then say why it matters to this client.
If the client can't repeat it back, it wasn't explained.
never: Promise that a fund will recover.

check.q: A client says, “This NFO is only ₹10, so it’s cheaper than the fund at ₹200.” What do you explain?
o: Agree — a lower NAV is always cheaper
NAV is the price of one unit; the same % growth gives the same rupee result, so judge by strategy, cost and fit, not NAV level
That NFOs are banned for new investors
check.why: Explains NAV as a price per unit; same % growth gives the same rupee result; judges by strategy, cost and fit, not NAV level.

check.q: A client’s SIP statement shows 45% after 3 years and they think that is 15% a year. What do you explain?
o: That 45% divided by 3 is the right yearly return
Absolute return ignores time; for a SIP the right annualised measure is XIRR, compared with the TRI benchmark
That SIP returns are never annualised
That only CAGR applies to SIPs
check.why: Explains absolute vs annualised return; shows XIRR as the right measure; compares with TRI benchmark.

check.q: A retiree wants the IDCW option “for monthly income”. What do you explain?
o: That IDCW is guaranteed monthly income
IDCW is paid from own capital, amount and timing not fixed; compare SWP for a chosen, regular amount; tax via CA
check.why: IDCW is paid from own capital, amount and timing not fixed; compares SWP for a chosen, regular amount; tax via CA.
